questions.q: What is the minimum acceptable haemoglobin concentration generally required before proceeding with an elective surgical procedure under general anaesthesia in Nigeria?
options: 7.0 g/dL (PCV 21%)
8.5 g/dL (PCV 25%)
questions.explain: For elective surgery, a haemoglobin of at least 10 g/dL (PCV 30%) is standard in most Nigerian surgical units to ensure adequate oxygen-carrying capacity, whereas emergency surgery may proceed at lower levels with simultaneous resuscitation and blood cover.

open.q: What minimum haemoglobin concentration and packed cell volume are traditionally required before elective surgery?
accept: 10 g/dL or PCV 30%
Haemoglobin of 10 g/dL
PCV of 30%

questions.q: Why must haemoglobin electrophoresis (genotype screening) be performed preoperatively in Nigerian surgical patients with unknown sickle cell status?
options: Perioperative hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration and hypothermia can precipitate sickling in susceptible patients
Patients with sickle trait cannot metabolise volatile anaesthetics
Sickle cell disease causes complete resistance to local anaesthetics
Haemoglobin S prevents blood cross-matching
questions.explain: Intraoperative hypoxia, cold theatre temperatures, dehydration, and tourniquet-induced stasis trigger polymerization of HbS in patients with HbSS or HbSC disease, leading to sickling crises, acute chest syndrome, or perioperative stroke.

open.q: Why is preoperative haemoglobin genotype testing essential before surgery in West African populations?
accept: To prevent perioperative sickling crises triggered by hypoxia, hypothermia, dehydration, or acidosis
To identify sickle cell disease or trait and prevent vaso-occlusive crisis during anaesthesia

questions.q: Which coagulation parameter is most sensitive for detecting extrinsic pathway dysfunction caused by obstructive jaundice or warfarin therapy?
options: Prothrombin time (PT) and International Normalized Ratio (INR)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
Bleeding time
Thrombin time
questions.explain: Obstructive jaundice impairs intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, reducing hepatic synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X. Because factor VII has the shortest half-life (4 to 6 hours) in the extrinsic pathway, PT/INR prolongs earliest.

open.q: Which coagulation test prolongs earliest in a patient with obstructive jaundice due to vitamin K malabsorption?
accept: Prothrombin time
PT and INR
International Normalized Ratio

questions.q: Which preoperative biochemical abnormality poses the highest immediate risk of fatal intraoperative cardiac arrhythmias?
options: Severe hyperkalaemia or hypokalaemia
Mild hyponatraemia of 133 mmol/L
Mildly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase
Borderline low serum albumin of 32 g/L
questions.explain: Serum potassium derangements alter myocardial resting membrane potential and conduction velocity; hyperkalaemia (especially above 6.0 mmol/L) risks asystole and is worsened by suxamethonium, while hypokalaemia predisposes to ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

open.q: Which serum electrolyte abnormality must be corrected prior to induction of anaesthesia because it precipitates life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias or asystole?
accept: Potassium abnormality
Hyperkalaemia or hypokalaemia
Serum potassium derangement

questions.q: What is the key difference between a 'Group and Save' request and a 'Cross-match' request before theatre?
options: Group and Save identifies blood group and screens antibodies; cross-match tests donor-recipient compatibility and reserves units
Group and Save takes hours, whereas cross-match takes seconds
Group and Save is for major haemorrhage; cross-match is only for low-risk surgery
Group and Save tests only donor blood, whereas cross-match tests only recipient blood
questions.explain: Group and Save (type and screen) identifies the patient's blood group and unexpected antibodies so compatible units can be issued rapidly if needed (for procedures with low expected blood loss), whereas full cross-matching allocates specific tested units for surgeries with significant expected blood loss.

open.q: How does a 'Group and Save' order differ practically from a full 'Cross-match' order before surgery?
accept: Group and Save types blood and screens antibodies without reserving specific units, whereas Cross-match tests donor blood against recipient serum and reserves units
Group and Save does not allocate specific donor units while Cross-match tests and reserves specific units

questions.q: Which imaging modality is the investigation of choice for rapidly detecting free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) in a suspected perforated peptic ulcer?
options: Erect chest radiograph showing free gas under the right hemidiaphragm
Supine abdominal radiograph showing psoas shadows
Abdominal ultrasound of the pelvis
Barium meal follow-through
questions.explain: An erect chest X-ray (after the patient sits upright for 10 to 15 minutes) detects as little as 1 to 2 mL of free subdiaphragmatic gas. If the patient cannot stand or sit, a left lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph is used.

open.q: Which plain radiograph view is ordered first to confirm pneumoperitoneum in a patient with suspected hollow viscus perforation?
accept: Erect chest X-ray
Erect chest radiograph
Upright chest X-ray

questions.q: Why is abdominal ultrasonography preferred over plain radiography as the initial imaging test in a patient presenting with surgical obstructive jaundice?
options: It reliably distinguishes extrahepatic biliary dilation from hepatocellular jaundice and detects gallstones without ionizing radiation
It provides high-resolution visualization of the retroperitoneal pancreas even in severe bowel gas
It directly measures serum conjugated bilirubin levels
It simultaneously extracts impacted common bile duct stones
questions.explain: Ultrasound is non-invasive, radiation-free, and highly sensitive for detecting intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile duct dilatation (surgical jaundice) and cholelithiasis, guiding whether MRCP, CT, or ERCP is required next.

open.q: What primary diagnostic distinction does an initial abdominal ultrasound make in a jaundiced surgical patient?
accept: It differentiates obstructive dilated bile ducts from non-obstructive hepatocellular jaundice
Detects biliary tract dilatation and gallstones to confirm obstructive jaundice

questions.q: Which clinical condition is an absolute contraindication to performing a barium enema or barium swallow?
options: Suspected gastrointestinal tract perforation
Chronic constipation
Mild gastro-oesophageal reflux
Iron deficiency anaemia
questions.explain: Leakage of barium sulphate into the mediastinum or peritoneal cavity causes severe, often fatal chemical mediastinitis or barium peritonitis with dense granulomatous adhesions. Water-soluble contrast (such as Gastrografin) must be used if perforation is suspected.

open.q: Why must barium sulphate contrast studies never be performed when gastrointestinal perforation is suspected?
accept: Extravasated barium causes severe chemical peritonitis or mediastinitis
Risk of fatal barium peritonitis or mediastinitis

questions.q: What key advantage does Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) have over core needle (Tru-Cut) biopsy, and what is its main limitation?
options: FNAC is quick and minimally invasive but yields cells without tissue architecture, limiting assessment of invasion
FNAC requires general anaesthesia, whereas core biopsy requires none
FNAC preserves full tissue architecture, whereas core biopsy yields only single cells
FNAC reliably establishes capsular invasion in follicular thyroid carcinoma
questions.explain: FNAC uses a fine 21G to 25G needle to sample cells quickly in the outpatient clinic, but because tissue architecture is lost, it cannot assess capsular/vascular invasion (e.g., follicular thyroid carcinoma) or stromal invasion (DCIS vs invasive breast cancer).

open.q: State the major pathological limitation of Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) compared with a core needle biopsy.
accept: It does not preserve tissue architecture and cannot differentiate in situ from invasive malignancy
Loss of histological architecture prevents assessment of tissue invasion

questions.q: According to the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification, how is a patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life categorized?
options: ASA Class IV
ASA Class II
ASA Class III
ASA Class V
questions.explain: ASA I is a normal healthy patient; ASA II has mild systemic disease; ASA III has severe systemic disease limiting activity; ASA IV has severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; ASA V is a moribund patient not expected to survive without operation; ASA VI is brain-dead.

open.q: What ASA physical status grade is assigned to a patient with severe systemic disease that poses a constant threat to life?
accept: ASA IV
ASA Class 4
Grade IV

questions.q: Which elements are legally and ethically required for valid informed surgical consent?
options: Decision-making capacity, full disclosure of diagnosis, proposed procedure, alternatives, and material risks, and voluntary agreement without coercion
Signature of a junior nurse alone without explaining surgical complications
Written consent signed after premedication sedation has already been administered
Verbal permission obtained exclusively from a neighbour when the adult patient is fully conscious
questions.explain: Valid informed consent requires a competent patient (or legal guardian for a minor) who receives clear information about the nature of the condition, intended operation, benefits, recognized risks, and alternatives, and consents freely while un-sedated.

open.q: List the three core ethical and legal pillars required for valid informed consent before surgery.
accept: Capacity, adequate information disclosure, and voluntariness
Competence, full disclosure of risks and alternatives, and voluntary consent

questions.q: An unconscious 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a ruptured spleen and haemorrhagic shock following a road traffic crash. No relatives are present. How should the surgical team proceed regarding consent?
options: Proceed immediately with life-saving laparotomy under the doctrine of necessity, documented by two doctors in the case notes
Delay surgery indefinitely until a blood relative arrives to sign the consent form
Obtain written consent from the ambulance driver
Administer intravenous fluids only and withhold surgery for 24 hours
questions.explain: When an adult lacks capacity in a life- or limb-threatening emergency and no legal proxy is available, surgeons act in the patient's best interests under the doctrine of necessity, clearly documenting the clinical justification.

open.q: Under what medico-legal principle may a surgeon operate immediately on an unconscious trauma patient with life-threatening bleeding when no next-of-kin is reachable?
accept: Doctrine of necessity
Emergency necessity in the patient's best interests
Principle of necessity

questions.q: What are the standard preoperative fasting guidelines ('6-4-2 rule') for healthy patients undergoing elective surgery?
options: 6 hours for solid food and non-human milk, 4 hours for breast milk, and 2 hours for clear fluids
12 hours for clear water and 24 hours for solid food
2 hours for solid meals and 6 hours for clear water
4 hours for solid food and 1 hour for cow's milk
questions.explain: The 6-4-2 fasting protocol minimizes gastric residual volume and pulmonary aspiration risk (Mendelson syndrome) while preventing dehydration and hypoglycaemia: 6 hours for solids/formula, 4 hours for breast milk, and 2 hours for clear fluids (water, black tea, pulp-free juice).

open.q: State the standard preoperative fasting intervals for solids, breast milk, and clear fluids under the 6-4-2 guideline.
accept: 6 hours for solids, 4 hours for breast milk, and 2 hours for clear fluids
Solids 6 hours, breast milk 4 hours, clear fluids 2 hours

questions.q: How should regular antihypertensive medications such as beta-blockers be managed on the morning of elective surgery?
options: Continue most chronic beta-blockers on the morning of surgery unless a specific contraindication exists
Stop all antihypertensives seven days before surgery
Double the beta-blocker dose immediately before induction
Replace oral beta-blockers with intravenous adrenaline
questions.explain: Antihypertensives (especially beta-blockers and clonidine), anticonvulsants, and inhalers should be continued up to and including the morning of surgery with a sip of water to avoid rebound tachycardia, hypertension, or seizures.

open.q: Why should a patient's regular beta-blocker therapy be continued with a sip of water on the morning of surgery rather than omitted?
accept: To prevent rebound hypertension, tachycardia, and perioperative myocardial ischaemia
Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and hypertension

questions.q: How many days before major elective surgery should aspirin or clopidogrel typically be discontinued when bleeding risk outweighs thrombotic risk?
options: 5 to 7 days
12 hours
24 hours
21 days
questions.explain: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet cyclooxygenase-1 and clopidogrel irreversibly blocks P2Y12 receptors for the entire 7-to-10-day lifespan of circulating platelets; stopping them 5 to 7 days preoperatively allows sufficient new functional platelets to be released.

open.q: How many days prior to elective surgery is clopidogrel or aspirin usually stopped to restore normal platelet aggregation, and why?
accept: 5 to 7 days, because they irreversibly inhibit platelets for their 7 to 10 day lifespan
7 days due to irreversible platelet inhibition

questions.q: Why must oral metformin be withheld before major surgery or procedures involving iodinated intravenous contrast?
options: Renal impairment around surgery or contrast exposure can reduce metformin clearance and increase lactic acidosis risk
Metformin causes profound intraoperative hyperglycaemia
Metformin blocks recovery from all neuromuscular blockers
Metformin routinely causes acute haemolytic anaemia
questions.explain: Metformin is excreted unchanged by the kidneys; perioperative dehydration, hypotension, or contrast-induced acute kidney injury causes drug accumulation and life-threatening metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA).

open.q: What serious metabolic complication can occur if metformin is continued in a surgical patient who develops perioperative dehydration or renal impairment?
accept: Lactic acidosis
Metformin-associated lactic acidosis

questions.q: A 60-year-old man who has taken oral prednisolone 15 mg daily for 2 years for rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for an elective hemicolectomy. What perioperative endocrine measure is required?
options: Provide perioperative glucocorticoid cover because chronic therapy may suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
Stop prednisolone abruptly 48 hours before surgery
Give propylthiouracil before induction
Restrict all sodium-containing intravenous fluids
questions.explain: Chronic exogenous corticosteroid therapy suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, preventing the endogenous cortisol surge needed for surgical stress and risking refractory hypotensive Addisonian crisis unless stress-dose hydrocortisone is given.

open.q: Why does a patient on long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy require perioperative intravenous hydrocortisone cover?
accept: To prevent acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis caused by HPA axis suppression during surgical stress
Chronic steroids suppress endogenous adrenal cortisol response to surgery

questions.q: When should prophylactic intravenous antibiotics ideally be administered for a clean-contaminated abdominal operation?
options: Within 30 to 60 minutes prior to skin incision (usually at induction of anaesthesia)
48 hours before admission to the surgical ward
Only after skin closure is completed
Continuously for 14 days postoperatively
questions.explain: Administering prophylactic antibiotics within 30 to 60 minutes before incision ensures peak bactericidal tissue and serum concentrations are present at the exact moment of bacterial contamination. Prolonged postoperative courses increase resistance and C. difficile infection.

open.q: What is the optimal timing for administering surgical antibiotic prophylaxis relative to the skin incision?
accept: Within 30 to 60 minutes before skin incision
At induction of anaesthesia within 60 minutes prior to incision

questions.q: Which combination provides effective mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis against deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in a high-risk pelvic cancer surgery patient?
options: Graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression plus low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin)
Strict bed rest for 5 days with high-dose vitamin K
Routine aspirin monotherapy started 2 weeks after discharge
Elevating the head of the bed by 60 degrees without leg movement
questions.explain: Combining mechanical methods (anti-embolism TED stockings and intraoperative intermittent pneumatic compression boots) with subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) addresses venous stasis and hypercoagulability in high-risk surgical patients.

open.q: Name one mechanical measure and one pharmacological agent commonly combined for perioperative venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.
accept: Graduated compression stockings (or intermittent pneumatic compression) and low-molecular-weight heparin
TED stockings and enoxaparin

questions.q: Why should preoperative hair removal from the surgical site be performed with electric clippers rather than a manual razor blade?
options: Razors create microscopic epidermal nicks that become colonized by skin bacteria and increase surgical site infection rates
Electric clippers sterilize the hair follicles permanently
Razors remove the entire stratum corneum and cause severe bleeding
Electric clippers eliminate the need for antiseptic skin preparation
questions.explain: Shaving with a razor the night before surgery causes micro-abrasions in the skin where Staphylococcus aureus proliferates, significantly raising surgical site infection rates. If hair removal is necessary, clipping immediately before surgery is recommended.

open.q: Why is shaving with a razor blade discouraged for preoperative hair removal compared with electric clipping just before surgery?
accept: Razors cause microscopic skin abrasions that harbour bacteria and increase surgical site infection risk
Micro-nicks from shaving promote bacterial colonization and wound infection

questions.q: Why is a skin site-marking arrow drawn with an indelible marker before the patient enters the operating theatre for paired organs or limbs?
options: To prevent wrong-site, wrong-side, or wrong-limb surgery
To outline the exact vascular supply of the skin flap
To guide the placement of the diathermy dispersive pad
To indicate the patient's blood group to the scrub nurse
questions.explain: Preoperative site marking on the awake patient (confirmed against consent forms and imaging) is a mandatory safety step to eliminate wrong-side or wrong-site procedures on limbs, eyes, kidneys, lungs, or inguinal hernias.

open.q: What catastrophic surgical error is prevented by marking the operative site with an indelible pen while the patient is still awake on the ward?
accept: Wrong-site surgery
Wrong-side or wrong-site operation

questions.q: What are the three sequential phases of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist?
options: Sign In (before induction of anaesthesia), Time Out (before skin incision), and Sign Out (before patient leaves the operating room)
Check In (at admission), Scrub Out (during closure), and Discharge (on the ward)
Induction, Intubation, and Extubation
Triage, Resuscitation, and Transfer
questions.explain: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist enforces team communication at three critical pauses: Sign In (before anaesthesia), Time Out (immediately before skin incision), and Sign Out (before the surgeon leaves the operating theatre).

open.q: Name the three stages of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist and state when each occurs.
accept: Sign In before induction of anaesthesia, Time Out before skin incision, and Sign Out before leaving the operating room
Sign In, Time Out, and Sign Out

questions.q: Where should the dispersive return plate (patient pad) for monopolar diathermy be placed during surgery?
options: Place it on clean, dry, well-perfused muscle with full skin contact, away from bony prominences and metal implants
Place it directly over a bony prominence such as the lateral malleolus
Place it over thick scar tissue or a metal prosthesis
Place it on wet skin beneath a pooled alcohol preparation
questions.explain: A large, well-vascularized muscle mass dissipates heat safely across the full surface area of the dispersive pad; bony prominences, scars, hair, or metal implants create uneven contact and high current density that cause diathermy pad burns.

open.q: List three site characteristics required for safe placement of a monopolar diathermy dispersive return plate.
accept: Clean, dry, hairless, well-vascularized muscular area away from bony prominences and metal implants
Well-vascularized muscle mass, hairless skin, and away from bone or metal prostheses

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of inflating a pneumatic limb tourniquet only after exsanguinating the limb with an Esmarch bandage or elevation?
options: To provide a bloodless surgical field while minimizing venous engorgement and blood loss
To permanently thrombose deep calf veins
To prevent nerve conduction so general anaesthesia is unnecessary
To warm the limb prior to orthopaedic osteotomy
questions.explain: Exsanguination drains venous blood from the extremity before tourniquet inflation (typically 50 to 100 mmHg above systolic BP in the upper limb and 100 to 150 mmHg above systolic BP in the lower limb), creating a clear bloodless field. Note that Esmarch exsanguination is avoided in infection, malignancy, or sickle cell disease.

open.q: Why is a limb exsanguinated prior to inflating a pneumatic surgical tourniquet, and name two contraindications to using an Esmarch exsanguination bandage?
accept: To obtain a bloodless field; contraindicated in limb infection, malignancy, DVT, or sickle cell disease
Creates a bloodless operative field; avoid in local infection, tumour, or sickle cell disease

questions.q: A 52-year-old man with gastric outlet obstruction from chronic duodenal ulceration has recurrent non-bilious vomiting. His serum electrolytes show Na+ 132 mmol/L, K+ 2.8 mmol/L, Cl- 84 mmol/L, and HCO3- 36 mmol/L. Which intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement is mandatory before taking him to theatre?
options: 0.9% normal saline with potassium chloride supplementation once urine output is established
5% dextrose in water without electrolytes
Sodium bicarbonate infusion to correct acidosis
Hypertonic 3% saline with loop diuretics
questions.explain: Gastric outlet obstruction causes loss of H+, Cl-, K+, and water, producing hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Resuscitation with 0.9% NaCl restores volume and chloride so the kidneys can excrete excess bicarbonate, alongside potassium replacement once urine flow is confirmed.

open.q: What characteristic acid-base and electrolyte abnormality occurs in gastric outlet obstruction, and which intravenous fluid is used to correct it preoperatively?
accept: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, corrected with 0.9% normal saline and potassium chloride
Hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis treated with normal saline and KCl
